segments.text: Email providers tell your app about
bounces, complaints, and incoming mail
by calling a webhook. That webhook is a
public URL. Anyone who finds it can post
a fake bounce and get a real customer
suppressed or post a fake inbound email
into your support queue.
In this video, how webhook signatures
work and how to verify them properly.
First, how signing works.
Most providers use the same idea. You
and the provider share a secret. For
each event, the provider computes an
HMAC of the timestamp and the body using
that secret. It sends the result in a
header alongside the timestamp. You
compute the same HMAC on your side. If
the two match, the event really came
from the provider and was not changed on
the way.
Now the code in Node.
Here is a typical verifier. The header
format differs between providers, so
check yours, but the steps are the same.
Split out the timestamp and the
signature. Reject anything older than 5
minutes. Recompute the HMAC over the
timestamp and the body.
Then compare with timing safe equal
after checking the length match, so an
attacker cannot learn the signature one
byte at a time from how long the
comparison takes.
Finally, the traps that break
verification.
Four mistakes come up again and again.
Parsing the JSON first, then signing a
re-serialized copy.
Whitespace and key order change, and the
signature never matches. Verify the raw
body exactly as it arrived. Comparing
signatures with triple equals, which
leaks timing. Use timing safe equal.
Skipping the timestamp. Without it,
someone who captures one valid event can
replay it forever. And committing the
secret to your repository. Keep it in
environment variables or a secrets
manager and rotate it if it leaks.
One more thing. Providers retry webhooks
that out, so the same event can arrive
twice.
Store each event's ID and skip the ones
you have already handled.
Verify the raw body, compare in constant
time, and check the timestamp. Next, we
keep our own sending under the
provider's rate limit.
